did_you_know.text: Did you know? The phrase “you shall surely listen” is a biblical way of intensifying the verb: to listen carefully and act accordingly.
Did you know? Mentioning both the city and the field presents the whole of life—from settlement life to work outside it.
Did you know? “The offspring of your cattle” refers to the young animals born to the herd, especially calves.
Did you know? “The increase of your flocks” is an ancient expression for abundant sheep; the word may be connected with Ashtoreth, an ancient fertility goddess.
Did you know? A “ṭene” was a basket, while a “mish’eret” was probably a bowl or container for dough or food.
Did you know? “When you come in and when you go out” is an inclusive expression describing a person throughout all journeys and activities.
Did you know? The numbers one and seven create a picture of complete scattering: the enemies arrive as one force but flee in every direction.
Did you know? “Storehouses” were grain storage buildings, so the blessing concerns not only growing crops but also preserving and managing them.
Did you know? In an agricultural society, being able to lend to others was a sign of economic independence and prosperity.
Did you know? “Head and not tail” is a metaphor for status and leadership, not a literal physical description.
Did you know? “Right and left” function here as a metaphor for straying from the path, much like saying “do not depart from the principle.”
Did you know? The verse piles up several different words—curse, confusion, and rebuke—to create a sense of troubles accumulating one after another.
Did you know? Some of the afflictions listed here are diseases of crops, such as blight and mildew; the Bible links human well-being with the health of the harvest.
Did you know? A sky of bronze and a ground of iron picture a severe drought: no rain comes from above, and the soil becomes hard below.
Did you know? Instead of rain falling from the sky, the verse describes dust and powder descending—a striking reversal of the image of blessing.
Did you know? “The boils of Egypt” recalls the plague of boils in the Exodus story, linking the warning to the national memory of Egypt.
Did you know? The examples of a betrothed woman, a house, and a vineyard show that war can destroy not only property but also relationships and plans for the future.
Did you know? Locusts were a serious agricultural threat in the ancient world because swarms could destroy entire fields very quickly.
Did you know? A vineyard requires years of work before producing a harvest, so losing its wine represents the waste of long-term labor.
Did you know? The Hebrew word nesher is usually translated as “eagle,” but it may also refer to another large bird of prey, such as a vulture.
Did you know? Walled cities were centers of defense and control in the ancient world, so a siege at their gates threatened the entire society.
Did you know? The phrase “every illness and every plague not written here” extends the warning even to afflictions not specifically listed.
Did you know? “An anxious heart” describes not just a passing emotion but an ongoing state of fear and unrest.
